newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean strike put off, but unrest still looms.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean strike put off, but unrest still looms.

text.p: Militant South Korean unionists called off a strike planned for Friday in protest at changes to the labour law, but the threat of industrial action still hung over the country's export industry.
The outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions had planned a four-hour walkout on Friday by its 500,000 members in 300 companies, including Hyundai Motor Co Ltd and Daewoo Heavy Industries Co.

A spokesman said the stoppage was put off since it now seemed unlikely that changes to the labour law allowing for layoffs and flexible work hours would be passed during the current session of parliament ending December 18.
"We have decided to postpone the earlier plan because we believe there is little chance that the law will be passed by parliament," Yoon Young-mo said.
On Thursday, opposition parties called for a delay in pushing through the bill. The ruling New Korea Party wants to adopt the legislation before parliament breaks up.
Yoon said the disagreement over the legislative timetable probably would stall passage of the bill.
However, the country's largest labour union umbrella organisation said it will go ahead with strikes planned for Monday and Thursday next week unless the government scraps the planned changes.
"There are no changes to our plans," said an official at the press office of the Federation of Korean Trade Unions.
"It depends on the labour law. If they don't cancel the changes, we will go ahead with our strikes."
The federation, which represents 1.2 million workers at 800 companies, plans a one-hour stoppage on Monday and a three-hour walkout on Thursday.
The outlawed confederation made clear it had not dropped its strike threat.
"Leaders of our member unions have been told to remain in close contact with the confederation so all our member workers can go on a strike at any time," Yoon said.
Originally, the confederation planned a nationwide indefinite strike from Monday.

Friday's four-hour strike was due to begin at 1.00 p.m. (0400 GMT). Instead, union meetings would be held at worksites around the country at that time to demand that labour changes be reversed, Yoon said.
He added that rallies by workers in Seoul and other cities would go ahead as planned on Saturday, a holiday.

The New Korea Party appealed to the union bodies on Thursday to drop plans for industrial action, saying it was "sympathetic" to workers but it was impossible to change the law to satisfy both labour and management.

Employer groups object to the first revisions to restrictive labour legislation in 43 years that would allow mulitiple unions in each workplace, a move they say would lead to greater militancy as labour unions vied for members.
South Korea was spurred to revise its labour laws by membership of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development. It formally joined the Paris-based club of rich nations on Thursday.
